en: Formerly, at the edge of Campā, dwelling on the banks of the pure lotus pond, the Teacher was engaged in bestowing grace upon the entire world;
he was questioned by one desiring an understanding of touch.
A monk named Ānanda recounted the life and activities of the people from the time of conception onwards.

In this world, the garment of birth is seen to be wonderfully variegated, with many frayed edges formed by the threads of the karma of embodied beings— threads that are white, black, or of mottled hue.
Even when it has grown old, one who is steeped in the oil of attachment, soiled by calamities, [seeks to preserve it] through various efforts.
He whose passion does not depart even after an exceedingly long period of transformation.
When the semen of the man, whose fortitude has dissolved, and the menses of the woman come together in union through the impact of an intense passion for touch,
they become one; by a certain law, this mixture then attains the state of a seed.
He who suddenly enters within it, like fire in close contact.
Like an outburst of passion entering a fragment of crystal, like the ocean’s water entering a cloud, like the fragrance of flowers entering a sesame seed, or like the heat of fire entering gold—
this very [impurity] enters the womb, its movement imperceptible even by those who are disciplined.
Like the wind being perfumed by various kinds of fragrances, he was being scented by manifold deeds.
In that state of the *mīnaparyuṣṭaka*, this subtle transformation of the sequence—
though possessing a variegated form with many diverse and abundant arrangements— is imperceptible; for a certain period of time, it carries on its modification while appearing as if devoid of change.
Like a peacock whose distinct markings are present within a peahen's egg as if it were composed of water.
There, having abandoned the successive stages beginning with the *ghana*, *kalala*, *tāśalya*, and *peśī* from the moment of conception, it is cooked by the heat generated within the womb;
then, after nine full months, this process of transformation reaches its completion.
Having fallen into the perception of suffering, he experiences some truly terrible affliction.
Like a fruit fallen of its own accord from its stalk at the proper time through the ripening of karma, he was driven by foul winds arising at that moment with irresistible force,
and was bound by the fetters of karma, which were accompanied by the objects of perception, habitual practice, and their underlying causes.
He was discharged like an arrow from within a bow, released by the mechanism.
With his face upturned and his tongue straightened, licking the tip of the nipple,
he drinks his mother’s milk— not with his ears nor with his eyes,
but with that which has become accustomed through the effort and exertion of practice since birth.
In his presence, that very latent impression (vāsanā), which ordains all manifestations, [appeared].
It is pervaded within by various types of sewn-in stitches that produce the flavor of diverse objects,
appearing like the spreading strands of a lotus fiber with its clearly visible threads.
Then, being deluded and receiving signals from his natural ministers—the senses—he recognizes the nurse through her breast-milk, speech, appearance, fragrance, and touch. (KAvk 10.9)
Tormented at every spot by insects with their grasping claws and the friction of bedding and clothing, his body trembling, and being devoured by worms,
he constantly cries out; yet, due to the absence of speech, he undergoes this physical mode of suffering.
Whom does he address, having become the abode of manifold calamities?
With his face sprinkled by the surging floods of milk vomited out due to the pain,
he appears drenched as it falls upon the surface of his upturned chest during the mature amorous play that steals away the memory of the illusory wife.
His entire body was completely pervaded by a shimmering radiance, as if with a smile.
Then, when he had mastered the science of writing, he effortlessly applied his hand to the drafting of the records of bondage within this cycle of existence;
beginning with the long syllable *Oṃ*, he wrote as if recording his own succession of births.
Intent upon the production of enjoyments, he bestows his intellect upon every group.
Having somehow attained wisdom as the delusion of childhood faded away, he once again lost his sense through the longing for desire in the subsequent stage of youth—
like flashes of lightning from clouds that sport amidst calamities in this essence-less world.
With a mind that has become even more firm, he fixes his attachment upon the amorous charms of women.
Directing his hearing toward their speech, his body toward the embrace of the moving women, his sense of smell toward the fragrance of the wine on their lips, his tasting toward its flavor,
and his sight toward their faces while holding the cup— he remained with all his activities suspended in sleep.
It maintains its measure, just as all the sense faculties do when they have undergone transformation into a subtle body.
He who hates what is dear, whose nature is habituated to constant aversion— he, the lustful man,
desiring ever-new delights, strives for another's beloved. Thus,
he is a witness to the embarrassment arising from mutual conduct that is unbecoming to each other.
His passion for the *citratantra* (the art of painting) is inherently distasteful and serves only as a source of ridicule.
For this man, who sinks and clings in the ocean of sense-objects that offers little support, and who has fallen like an elephant with its progress obstructed in the mud,
a swoon of delusion arises, devoid of any knowledge of what ought to be done.
He was led into blindness by youth that lasts but a few days.
As long as he wanders, moves about, takes pleasure, yawns, and speaks with ever-increasing smiles, his limbs writhing in the embrace of passion—
for that long, the one released by Time shall surely fall upon him.
A garland of victims under the guise of hoary hair white with frost.
From time to time, under the influence of the sleep of delusion and through the passing of moments, he reflects with sorrow:
"In this body, no merit has been acquired, nor given, nor enjoyed;
thus, like one robbed by thieves, he suffers."
For those who are utterly deluded, that negligence results in the fruit of their latent tendencies.
When that springtime of lovely women and flowering creepers had passed— youth, which is like a dream and equal in its fleeting nature to wealth acquired through evil deeds—
he was one whose entire natural disposition had vanished, his limbs exhausted by all those who were now indifferent to him.
Then, like a king fallen from his kingdom, he grieves for the past with sorrow.
Life has been spent, yet nothing worthy was bestowed upon the beggar; fame has not been raised in every direction, nor has the path of the righteous been followed;
instead, the poison of begging has been drunk, resulting in the onset of intense and chilling distress.
"Since I was afraid of sin, I did not do anything at all; that very thing has now been brought about."
Where is that enchanting beauty of youth, which steals the luster of golden trees? And where is this body, its radiance faded like a tree struck by worms?
From afar, these young women have avoided my gaze, their eyes hidden within the corners.
They speak of me as a monkey in the forest at a tree that is withered and cold.
This very body, a phantom form, does not at all succumb to dissolution; all those teeth-jewels have fallen away, yet there is no fault in them;
the wind strikes against the vigor of the limbs, yet it does not strike at the sprout of delusion.
This is the exhaustion of my craving, even though I am lying down here as one whose life is spent.
Having thus reflected, afflicted by spreading, uneven gasps and hiccups,
he was suddenly intent on abandoning the worldly course long familiar to him; rendered mute and his fortitude shattered, he brooded upon the separation from his kinsmen.
Like a great debt incurred through the exhaustion of one's power, he is impoverished when his time has come.
At the time when life reaches its end, he perceives with his intellect the earth, home, wealth, attendants, children, wife, and other things—
just as much as he does even during his lifetime through the continuous bonds of affection and delusion.
Through various means, having cultivated intimacy within, one attains the state of being identical with that.
Having experienced suffering produced by unbearable evil karma within thousands of cauldrons, one wanders through various wombs in the Raurava and Kālasūtra hells;
or else, that state of happiness acquired through even a fraction of merit becomes a source of suffering when it is exhausted.
Therefore, let the one of pure intellect apply themselves toward the attainment of the fruit of the non-returner.
Thus, having taken a vow to ferry beings across the terrifying ocean of existence,
the Blessed One instructed them for the sake of attaining virtue.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Descent into the Womb," in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
